title: Interim Study of Procedures for Investigating the Effect of Light on Impression and Behavior
research_question: To what extent do variations in environmental lighting affect human behavior and user impressions, and can new study methods (Semantic Differential rating scales, Multidimensional Scaling, and observational mapping) be useful techniques for lighting research?

participants.description: Adult subjects, well distributed in age and educational background. 96 subjects for rating scales (12 groups of 8), and 46 subjects for multidimensional scaling. Uninstructed subjects for observational studies.
participants.recruitment: Accessed through the General Electric Lighting Institute at Nela Park in Cleveland.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Six different lighting arrangements in a medium-sized conference room. Arrangements varied in overhead downlighting (low/high intensity), peripheral wall-lighting, and diffuse overhead lighting (low/high setting). A separate 'restaurant-type setting' (coffee bar) was used for seat selection observations.

measures.instrument: Osgood-type Semantic Differential rating scales (34 scales)
Pairwise comparison ratings (0-10 scale for degree of change)

findings.antecedent: Six different lighting arrangements (initial exposure)
findings.consequent: Subjective impressions (17 of 34 Semantic Differential rating scales)
findings.mechanism: Lighting variations alter the information content of the visual field, leading to differential initial impressions.
findings.quote: 17 (of 34) rating scales showed a significant difference in response to the room under the six lighting arrangements.

findings.antecedent: Six different lighting arrangements (comparative ratings)
findings.consequent: Subjective impressions (all 34 Semantic Differential rating scales)
findings.mechanism: Providing a frame of reference (comparative ratings) enhanced the effectiveness of rating scales without altering the basic nature of judgments.
findings.quote: all of the 34 rating scales showed a significant difference in impression between two or more of the six lighting arrangements

findings.antecedent: Lighting arrangement 6 (combination: overhead downlighting + peripheral wall-lighting + overhead diffuse) and 4 (combination: overhead downlighting + end walls)
findings.mechanism: Specific lighting patterns (e.g., non-uniform, peripheral) are associated with more positive evaluative impressions.
findings.quote: lighting arrangements 6 and 4 were generally most preferred

findings.antecedent: Lighting arrangement 3 (overhead diffuse, low setting) and 5 (overhead diffuse, high intensity)
findings.mechanism: Overhead diffusing systems, regardless of intensity, are associated with less positive evaluative impressions.
findings.quote: arrangements 3 and 5 were least preferred.

findings.antecedent: Lighting arrangement 5 (overhead diffuse, high intensity) and 6 (combination: overhead downlighting + peripheral wall-lighting + overhead diffuse)
findings.mechanism: Higher photic energy and specific lighting distributions (e.g., peripheral wall-lighting) contribute to impressions of clarity and brightness.
findings.quote: lighting arrangements 5 and 6 were grouped as the clearest, brightest, etc.

findings.antecedent: Lighting arrangement 1 (overhead downlighting, low intensity), 2 (peripheral wall-lighting, all walls), 3 (overhead diffuse, low setting), and 4 (combination: overhead downlighting + end walls)
findings.mechanism: Lesser photic energy and certain lighting distributions are associated with lower perceptual clarity.
findings.quote: arrangements 1, 2, 3, and 4 represented lesser photic energy.

findings.antecedent: Lighting arrangement 1 (overhead downlighting, low intensity) and 3 (overhead diffuse, low setting)
findings.mechanism: Low intensity overhead arrangements with subdued wall brightness induce a feeling of less spaciousness.
findings.quote: Lighting arrangements 1 and 3 were judged significantly less spacious than arrangements 6 and 2.

findings.antecedent: Lighting arrangement 6 (combination: overhead downlighting + peripheral wall-lighting + overhead diffuse) and 2 (peripheral wall-lighting, all walls)
findings.mechanism: Lighting all four walls (peripheral lighting) induces a feeling of greater spaciousness.
findings.quote: lighting all four walls (as in arrangements 6 and 2) seemed to induce a feeling of greater spaciousness

findings.antecedent: Change in light intensity from low (Arrangement 3) to high (Arrangement 5) in overhead diffusing systems
findings.mechanism: Intensity of light emission from overhead diffusing systems has little effect on general evaluative impressions like pleasantness or friendliness.
findings.quote: changing only light intensity had a negligible effect on general 'evaluative impressions.'

findings.antecedent: Change in light intensity from low (Arrangement 3) to high (Arrangement 5) in overhead diffusing systems
findings.mechanism: Higher intensity leads to impressions of greater clarity, brightness, and distinctness.
findings.quote: the higher intensity system (arrangement 5) was rated as most clear, bright, and distinct

findings.antecedent: Higher brightness levels (Arrangement 5 vs 3)
findings.mechanism: Higher brightness levels induce an impression of increased spaciousness.
findings.quote: higher brightness levels tended to produce an impression of increased 'spaciousness.'

findings.antecedent: Change in light distribution from downlighting (Arrangement 1) to overhead diffuse (Arrangement 3) at 10 fc
findings.mechanism: Both downlighting and overhead diffuse systems at low intensity produce similar, negative impressions of perceptual clarity.
findings.quote: arrangements 1 and 3 (each at 10 fc... ) produced a roughly similar impression regarding 'perceptual clarity;'

findings.antecedent: Downlighting (Arrangement 1) vs. overhead diffuse (Arrangement 3) at 10 fc
findings.mechanism: Downlighting consistently produces more positive evaluative impressions than overhead diffuse lighting at the same low intensity.
findings.quote: arrangement 1 (downlighting) consistently produced more positive 'evaluative impressions' than arrangement 3.

findings.antecedent: Downlighting (Arrangement 1) vs. overhead diffuse (Arrangement 3) at 10 fc
findings.mechanism: Differences in lighting distribution (downlighting vs. overhead diffuse) at low intensity can marginally affect impressions of spaciousness.
findings.quote: There were also marginally significant differences in the impression of 'spaciousness.'

findings.antecedent: Limited wall lighting added to low intensity overhead lighting (Arrangement 4 vs 1)
findings.mechanism: Adding limited wall lighting enhances positive evaluative impressions.
findings.quote: arrangement 4 (downlights plus wall lights) was consistently evaluated more positively than arrangement 1 (downlights only).

findings.antecedent: Limited wall lighting added to low intensity overhead lighting (Arrangement 4 vs 1)
findings.mechanism: Adding limited wall lighting improves perceptual clarity.
findings.quote: The limited wall lighting also improved 'perceptual clarity' somewhat

findings.antecedent: Limited wall lighting added to low intensity overhead lighting (Arrangement 4 vs 1)
findings.mechanism: Adding limited wall lighting significantly affects the impression of spaciousness.
findings.quote: and significantly affected the impression of 'spaciousness.'

findings.antecedent: Lighting arrangements
findings.mechanism: Subjects respond to lighting variations along three primary perceptual dimensions: bright/dim, uniform/non-uniform, and peripheral/overhead.
findings.quote: there were three primary dimensions of perceptual experience to which the subjects could or did respond: (1) bright/dim, (2) uniform/non-uniform, and (3) peripheral/overhead.

findings.antecedent: Lighting arrangements
findings.mechanism: The 'bright/dim' dimension from MDS is highly correlated with the perceptual clarity factor from Semantic Differential ratings.
findings.quote: A correlation of 0.99 between the perceptual clarity SD ratings and the 'bright/dim' INDSCAL dimension was achieved

findings.antecedent: Lighting arrangements
findings.mechanism: Evaluative impressions are well represented by a linear combination of 'overhead/peripheral' and 'uniform/non-uniform' MDS dimensions.
findings.quote: a correlation of 0.92 was obtained in the second step, using both the 'overhead/peripheral' and 'uniform/non-uniform' dimensions as predictors

findings.antecedent: Lighting arrangements
findings.mechanism: Impressions of spaciousness are well represented by a linear combination of 'uniform/non-uniform,' 'overhead/peripheral,' and 'bright-dim' MDS dimensions.
findings.quote: a multiple regression coefficient to 0.98.

findings.antecedent: Diffuse overhead lighting (Arrangement 3 and 5)
findings.consequent: Negative evaluative judgments and overt negative behaviors (e.g., 'thumbs down', squinting, eye rubbing)
findings.mechanism: Lighting conditions perceived as unflattering or uncomfortable trigger negative affective and behavioral responses.
findings.quote: Diffuse overhead lighting arrangements 3 and 5 elicited generally negative evaluative judgments on the rating scales.

findings.antecedent: Low intensity down-lighting (Arrangement 1)
findings.consequent: Variability in rating responses and cued associations (night club vs. church-like)
findings.mechanism: Ambiguous or low-intensity lighting can cue different contextual associations, leading to varied interpretations and responses.
findings.quote: subject comments suggested that this lighting arrangement cued two very different types of associations.

findings.antecedent: High contrast lighting arrangements (coffee bar setting, Fig 10-A)
findings.consequent: Seat selection patterns (orientation toward light/entrance stair)
findings.mechanism: Lighting cues can direct attention and influence seating choices, orienting occupants towards areas of activity or visual interest.
findings.quote: most of those first approaching an empty table... would tend to select a seat which oriented them toward the light.

findings.antecedent: Modified lighting arrangement (wall-lighting opposite entrance, Fig 10-B)
findings.consequent: Seat selection patterns (orientation toward interior of room, away from entrance)
findings.mechanism: Altering lighting distribution can dramatically change spatial affordances and redirect occupant behavior, such as seat selection.
findings.quote: there was a strong tendency for subjects approaching an empty table to select seats in a different manner-now facing the interior of the room

mechanisms: Light as a vehicle that facilitates selective visual processing and alters the information content of the visual field.
Lighting design establishes cues that facilitate or alter user understanding of the environment and activities.
Induced psychological effects from lighting variations (e.g., spaciousness).
Lighting conditions cue different types of associations (e.g., night club vs. church-like).
Lighting conditions induce instinctive or learned tendencies in overt behavior.
moderators: Individual differences in response modes (1D, 2D, 3D perceivers in MDS).
implementation_implications: Lighting variables induce consistent and shared impressions for users.
Rating scales and multidimensional scaling are useful techniques for gaining insight into lighting phenomena.
Lighting design decisions (intensity, distribution, wall lighting) have predictable subjective implications for evaluative impressions, perceptual clarity, and spaciousness.
Lighting variations influence overt behavior, such as gestures, comments, and seat selection patterns.
Realistic studies of lighting quality and value may depend on understanding the system's function as a device for communicating ideas or reinforcing appropriate impressions for the user.

Mean ratings of six lighting arrangements on Factor 1 (Evaluative), Factor 2 (Perceptual Clarity), and Factor 4 (Spaciousness) scales, focusing on distribution changes.
Mean ratings of six lighting arrangements on Factor 1 (Evaluative), Factor 2 (Perceptual Clarity), and Factor 4 (Spaciousness) scales, focusing on adding wall lighting.

limitations: Findings are tentative, representing limited samples of lighting variables.
The location of the room at G.E.'s Lighting Institute might have cued subjects to the likelihood that lighting manipulations were of interest, potentially influencing initial ratings.
The 'warm-cool' variation in light tone was confounded with the 'uniform/non-uniform' variation in MDS Dimension 2.
Individual differences in response modes may reflect real differences in visual perception or limited capacity for information processing.
